title: Coastal flooding possible as rain, wind, king tides converge on B.C.: Environment Canada | CBC News
html:
British Columbia·Updated

'Significant' wind, waves and rain forecast for coastal B.C.: Environment Canada

Coastal flooding warnings in effect for parts of Vancouver Island, Central Coast, Haida Gwaii

More rainy, windy weather is expected along parts of the B.C. coast, coinciding with a run of king tides, according to Environment and Climate Change Canada.

The federal department has issued coastal flooding warnings for parts of the Central Coast, western Vancouver Island and Haida Gwaii. It says a moderate storm surge and large waves will come alongside very high tides, known as king tides, Tuesday through Thursday.

Together, they could elevate water levels 20 to 50 centimetres above the highest astronomical tides, Environment Canada says.

A coastal flooding statement is also in effect for parts of the South Coast, with water levels expected to rise and peak on Thursday.

The District of Squamish has declared a state of local emergency in light of the incoming weather, while some areas on the west coast of Vancouver Island close public beach access amid high tides.

Rainfall amounts of up to 200 millimetres are expected on some parts of Vancouver Island, and some higher amounts are possible locally, according to Environment Canada.

"Rainfall rates will ease Wednesday morning but another potent storm arrives late Wednesday afternoon bringing a new round of significant precipitation and strong winds."

The Delta neighbourhood of Boundary Bay saw king tides on Tuesday, as the coastal community braces for storms that are set to swell the waters. (Hunter Soo/CBC)

State of local emergency

The District of Squamish said in an update that it had set up a station where residents could pick up sandbags and crews were constructing sandbag walls to prevent water from entering the downtown area.

The Sea-to-Sky region was pummeled by a series of storms earlier this month, with a number of deaths along waterways related to high river flows in the region.

Communities like Delta, farther south, were also providing residents with sandbags and shoring up low-lying areas on Tuesday.

"Some houses are far more protected than others in the area. And our staff are very familiar ... they know where they need to go and support residents who are at highest risk of those storm surges," Melissa Granum, the city's mayor, said Tuesday.

Delta Mayor Melissa Granum is seen on Nov. 24, 2026. (Martin Diotte/Radio-Canada)

Environment Canada is warning landslides could occur in vulnerable areas such as steep slopes, deforested areas or recent burn scars.

In Tofino, on the west coast of Vancouver Island, the district said Tuesday it may intermittently close public access to its popular beaches over the following days as a safety precaution.

Nearby Ucluelet announced it would close its beaches and trails until further notice.

"At noon [on Tuesday] we were observing swells and waves hitting the shore that were anywhere from 20 to 25 feet in height with fairly regular consistency," Ucluelet Fire Chief Mike Walroth said.

He added that the tides were throwing up driftwood onto beaches and trails, damaging fences in the process.

Debris on the road near Tlell, B.C., in Haida Gwaii led to Highway 16 being closed on Tuesday afternoon. Haida Gwaii is among the areas with a coastal flooding warning on Tuesday. (DriveBC)

Wind warnings are also in effect for parts of Vancouver Island and the Sunshine Coast.

Gusts could reach 110 km/h at times in certain areas.

Local utility outages are possible, according to Environment Canada, and residents are urged to secure loose objects.

As of 3 p.m. PT on Tuesday, just under 10,000 B.C. Hydro customers across the province had lost power, according to the utility.

High winds created big waves that smashed drift logs into the Ross Bay walkway in Victoria on Tuesday. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

The River Forecast Centre has issued a high streamflow advisory for Vancouver Island and the South Coast, as rivers are "expected to rise rapidly in response to rainfall."

Jonathan Boyd, a hydrologist for the River Forecast Centre, said rivers have been high due to the atmospheric river about two weeks ago that was particularly focused on Vancouver Island.

"What we're seeing here now is another punch, that's kind of a one-two punch," Boyd said, adding that another, stronger system is expected late Wednesday through Thursday.

The Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation on the west coast of Vancouver Island has issued an evacuation alert for some properties along the shoreline due to flooding. Anyone in the affected area must be ready to leave at a moment's notice.

In Parksville, north of Nanaimo, an evacuation alert was issued for some low-lying areas on Tuesday — which included some RV resorts, a curling club, hotels and other properties along the coast.

With files from Patrick Swadden, Pinki Wong and Shaurya Kshatri
summary: The District of Squamish has declared a state of local emergency in light of the incoming weather, with areas on the west coast of Vancouver Island closing public beach access amid high tides.
